title: Literature & Style
subtitle: Read the literary tenses, name the figures of speech and hear what the text leaves unsaid

lessons.title: Le passé simple
lessons.description: Recognise the passé simple and the other literary tenses that carry French narration.

blocks.heading: A tense you read rather than speak
blocks.body: The passé simple is the tense of written narration: novels, short stories, fairy tales, history books and the narrative passages of quality journalism. In conversation the same events would be told in the passé composé. Nobody will ask you to produce it spontaneously at C1, but you must decode it instantly, because a page of literary French can contain thirty forms of it.

examples.french: Il entra sans frapper et posa sa valise contre le mur.
examples.english: He came in without knocking and set his suitcase against the wall.
examples.note: spoken French: il est entré, il a posé

examples.french: Le roi mourut en hiver ; le royaume changea de visage.
examples.english: The king died in winter; the kingdom changed its face.

examples.french: Nous partîmes à l'aube et personne ne nous vit.
examples.english: We left at dawn and nobody saw us.
examples.note: the nous form is the surest signal of the passé simple

examples.french: Ils comprirent trop tard ce que la lettre annonçait.
examples.english: They understood too late what the letter was announcing.

examples.french: Elle sourit, puis se tut pour toujours.
examples.english: She smiled, then fell silent forever.
examples.note: sourit is identical in the present and the passé simple — context decides

blocks.tip: If a narrative text uses the passé simple, it will almost never slip into the passé composé. A sudden passé composé inside such a text is a deliberate effect: the narrator steps out of the story to speak to you.

blocks.heading: The three shapes of the ending
blocks.body: Almost every passé simple falls into one of three vowel families. Verbs in -er take an a-shape, most verbs in -ir and -re take an i-shape, and a large closed group of irregulars takes a u-shape. The circumflex on the nous and vous forms is the signature of the tense.

examples.french: je parlai, tu parlas, il parla, nous parlâmes, vous parlâtes, ils parlèrent
examples.english: I spoke, you spoke, he spoke, we spoke, you spoke, they spoke
examples.note: a-shape: all -er verbs, including aller (il alla)

examples.french: je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finîmes, vous finîtes, ils finirent
examples.english: I finished, you finished, he finished, we finished, you finished, they finished
examples.note: i-shape: finir, partir, prendre (il prit), écrire (il écrivit)

examples.french: je courus, tu courus, il courut, nous courûmes, vous courûtes, ils coururent
examples.english: I ran, you ran, he ran, we ran, you ran, they ran
examples.note: u-shape: courir, savoir (il sut), vouloir (il voulut), lire (il lut), vivre (il vécut)

examples.french: Il fut, elle eut, ils firent, elle vint, il tint.
examples.english: He was, she had, they did, she came, he held.
examples.note: the five you meet on every page: être, avoir, faire, venir, tenir

examples.french: L'enfant naquit un soir de novembre et vécut cent ans.
examples.english: The child was born one November evening and lived a hundred years.
examples.note: naître → naquit, vivre → vécut

blocks.tip: The -èrent ending belongs only to -er verbs; -irent and -urent cover everything else. Spotting the vowel tells you which infinitive to look for.

blocks.heading: Foreground and background
blocks.body: The passé simple moves the story forward: each verb is a new event, complete and bounded. The imparfait stops the clock to describe the setting, the habits, the weather, the state of mind. Reading a literary page well means seeing which sentences advance the plot and which merely hold the camera still.

examples.french: La pluie tombait depuis trois jours quand le voyageur frappa à la porte.
examples.english: Rain had been falling for three days when the traveller knocked at the door.
examples.note: imparfait = backdrop, passé simple = the event

examples.french: Il faisait froid ; elle resserra son châle et pressa le pas.
examples.english: It was cold; she pulled her shawl tighter and quickened her pace.

examples.french: Chaque soir, il relisait la même lettre. Un jour, il la brûla.
examples.english: Every evening he would reread the same letter. One day he burned it.
examples.note: habit in the imparfait, rupture in the passé simple

examples.french: Le village dormait encore lorsque la nouvelle se répandit.
examples.english: The village was still asleep when the news spread.

examples.french: Elle crut d'abord à une plaisanterie, puis elle comprit.
examples.english: At first she thought it was a joke, then she understood.
examples.note: two successive events: croire → crut, comprendre → comprit

blocks.tip: A useful test: if you could add "soudain" or "à ce moment-là", the verb is probably a passé simple.

items.example: Le récit s'ouvre sur une scène de départ.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrative opens on a departure scene.

items.example: La narration alterne entre deux époques.
items.exampleEnglish: The narration alternates between two periods.

items.example: Le narrateur ne dit jamais son nom.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrator never gives his name.

items.example: Le romancier laisse au lecteur le soin de conclure.
items.exampleEnglish: The novelist leaves it to the reader to conclude.

items.example: Le conte commence toujours par une formule rituelle.
items.exampleEnglish: The tale always begins with a ritual formula.

items.example: Une nouvelle bien construite tient en vingt pages.
items.exampleEnglish: A well-built short story fits into twenty pages.

items.example: Le chapitre s'achève sur une question sans réponse.
items.exampleEnglish: The chapter ends on an unanswered question.

items.example: L'intrigue se noue dès les premières pages.
items.exampleEnglish: The plot is tied up from the very first pages.

items.example: Le protagoniste refuse le rôle qu'on lui assigne.
items.exampleEnglish: The main character refuses the role assigned to him.

items.example: Une dernière péripétie relance le récit.
items.exampleEnglish: One last twist restarts the narrative.

items.example: Le dénouement laisse un goût amer.
items.exampleEnglish: The ending leaves a bitter taste.

items.english: the opening lines of a work
items.example: L'incipit installe aussitôt une atmosphère de menace.
items.exampleEnglish: The opening lines immediately establish an atmosphere of menace.

items.example: L'épilogue nous ramène trente ans plus tard.
items.exampleEnglish: The epilogue takes us back thirty years later.

items.example: Le passé simple appartient au récit écrit.
items.exampleEnglish: The passé simple belongs to written narrative.

items.example: Le passé antérieur suit presque toujours « dès que ».
items.exampleEnglish: The past anterior almost always follows "dès que".

items.example: L'imparfait plante le décor du récit.
items.exampleEnglish: The imperfect sets the scene of the narrative.

items.example: Le plus-que-parfait rappelle ce qui précède l'action.
items.exampleEnglish: The pluperfect recalls what precedes the action.

items.example: La terminaison en -èrent signale un verbe du premier groupe.
items.exampleEnglish: The -èrent ending signals a first-group verb.

items.example: Le radical du passé simple de « venir » est irrégulier.
items.exampleEnglish: The passé simple stem of "venir" is irregular.

items.example: Sa conjugaison surprend, mais la forme est correcte.
items.exampleEnglish: Its conjugation is surprising, but the form is correct.

items.example: L'auteur narre ces événements sans jamais les juger.
items.exampleEnglish: The author narrates these events without ever judging them.

items.example: Le chroniqueur relate la scène avec une froideur étudiée.
items.exampleEnglish: The chronicler relates the scene with studied coldness.

items.example: L'accident survint au moment où nul ne l'attendait.
items.exampleEnglish: The accident occurred at the moment when nobody expected it.

items.example: « Enfin ! » s'écria-t-elle en ouvrant la lettre.
items.exampleEnglish: "At last!" she cried, opening the letter.

items.example: Il songea longuement à ce qu'il venait d'entendre.
items.exampleEnglish: He pondered at length what he had just heard.

items.english: to fall silent, to say nothing
items.example: Elle se tut et regarda la fenêtre.
items.exampleEnglish: She fell silent and looked at the window.

items.english: to loom up, to appear suddenly
items.example: Une silhouette surgit de la brume.
items.exampleEnglish: A silhouette loomed up out of the mist.

items.example: Il franchit le seuil sans se retourner.
items.exampleEnglish: He crossed the threshold without turning round.

items.example: La voiture s'éloigna dans un nuage de poussière.
items.exampleEnglish: The car moved away in a cloud of dust.

items.example: Il aperçut une lumière au bout du couloir.
items.exampleEnglish: He caught sight of a light at the end of the corridor.

items.example: La maison demeura vide pendant vingt ans.
items.exampleEnglish: The house remained empty for twenty years.

items.example: Ils se mirent en route avant l'aube.
items.exampleEnglish: They set off before dawn.

items.example: Au crépuscule, le village retrouvait son silence.
items.exampleEnglish: At dusk, the village recovered its silence.

items.example: Jadis, ce chemin menait à la mer.
items.exampleEnglish: Long ago, this path led to the sea.

items.example: Naguère encore, on lisait ce roman dans toutes les écoles.
items.exampleEnglish: Not so long ago, this novel was read in every school.

items.example: Aussitôt dit, aussitôt fait.
items.exampleEnglish: No sooner said than done.

blocks.heading: Le passé antérieur: the event before the event
blocks.body: The passé antérieur is built with the passé simple of avoir or être plus a past participle. It appears almost exclusively after a time conjunction — dès que, lorsque, quand, après que, à peine ... que — to mark an action completed just before the next one. In speech, the plus-que-parfait or the passé surcomposé takes its place.

examples.french: Dès qu'il eut terminé sa lettre, il sortit la poster.
examples.english: As soon as he had finished his letter, he went out to post it.
examples.note: eut terminé = passé antérieur, sortit = passé simple

examples.french: Quand elle fut partie, la maison parut immense.
examples.english: When she had left, the house seemed immense.
examples.note: être verbs agree: fut partie

examples.french: À peine eurent-ils franchi le pont que l'orage éclata.
examples.english: Scarcely had they crossed the bridge than the storm broke.
examples.note: à peine at the head of the clause triggers inversion

examples.french: Après qu'il eut parlé, plus personne n'osa répondre.
examples.english: After he had spoken, nobody dared reply any longer.

examples.french: Lorsque le jour se fut levé, ils reprirent la route.
examples.english: When day had broken, they set off again.

blocks.tip: Reading trick: eut / fut + participle is the passé antérieur; avait / était + participle is the plus-que-parfait. One belongs to literature, the other to everyday French.

blocks.heading: The other literary forms you will meet
blocks.body: Nineteenth-century prose and formal contemporary writing also use the imparfait du subjonctif (qu'il parlât, qu'elle vînt, qu'il fût) and the plus-que-parfait du subjonctif, which can double as a literary conditional — the so-called deuxième forme du conditionnel passé. You only need to recognise them and translate them into ordinary French in your head.

examples.french: Il fallait qu'elle partît avant la nuit.
examples.english: She had to leave before nightfall.
examples.note: modern French: qu'elle parte

examples.french: Le juge exigea qu'on lui remît le dossier.
examples.english: The judge demanded that the file be handed over to him.
examples.note: modern French: qu'on lui remette

examples.french: Il eût aimé revoir la mer une dernière fois.
examples.english: He would have liked to see the sea one last time.
examples.note: eût aimé = aurait aimé

examples.french: Nul n'eût osé le contredire.
examples.english: Nobody would have dared contradict him.
examples.note: literary equivalent of n'aurait osé

examples.french: On l'aurait cru mort si sa main n'eût tremblé.
examples.english: One would have thought him dead had his hand not trembled.
examples.note: n'eût tremblé = n'avait pas tremblé

blocks.tip: The circumflex distinguishes two look-alikes: il fut is the passé simple (he was), il fût is the imparfait du subjonctif. One tiny accent, two different grammars.

items.prompt: Listen. Which tense carries the main action?
items.french: La nuit tombait quand il poussa la porte de l'auberge.

items.prompt: Listen. What is the infinitive of the verb in the passé simple?
items.french: Elle ne sut jamais pourquoi il était revenu.

items.prompt: Listen and write the sentence.
items.french: Ils partirent au lever du jour.
items.answer: Ils partirent au lever du jour.
acceptedAnswers: ils partirent au lever du jour
Ils partirent au lever du jour

items.prompt: Dictation: a sentence in the passé antérieur.
items.french: Dès qu'il eut fermé le livre, le silence retomba.
items.answer: Dès qu'il eut fermé le livre, le silence retomba.
acceptedAnswers: des qu'il eut ferme le livre le silence retomba
Dès qu'il eut fermé le livre le silence retomba
des qu il eut ferme le livre le silence retomba

items.prompt: Read this narrative sentence aloud.
items.french: Il traversa la place déserte et disparut sous les arcades.
items.english: He crossed the deserted square and vanished under the arcades.
items.tip: Traversa ends in a clean open -a: trah-vehr-SAH. Never pronounce a final -t in disparut (dees-pah-RU).

items.prompt: Say the nous form of the passé simple.
items.french: Nous descendîmes l'escalier sans allumer la lumière.
items.english: We went down the staircase without turning on the light.
items.tip: The circumflex does not lengthen much here: say day-sahn-DEEM, with a crisp final -m sound.

items.prompt: Read a sentence with the literary conditional.
items.french: Nul n'eût imaginé qu'elle revînt un jour.
items.english: Nobody would have imagined that she would return one day.
items.tip: Eût is simply "u", with rounded lips; the liaison gives nul-nu-tee-mah-zhee-NAY.

passages.title: Le retour à Villebranche
passages.french:
Le train le déposa à Villebranche un peu avant midi, sous un ciel bas qui promettait la pluie.
Rien n'avait changé, et pourtant tout lui parut plus petit : la gare, la place, les deux platanes.
Il posa sa valise sur le banc, puis se ravisa et la reprit aussitôt.
Personne ne l'attendait ; il n'avait prévenu personne.
La rue montait vers l'église, comme autrefois, entre des façades que le soleil avait pâlies.
Une femme balayait son seuil ; elle leva la tête, le regarda passer et ne le reconnut pas.
Il en éprouva un soulagement qu'il n'osa pas s'avouer.
Devant la maison, il s'arrêta : les volets étaient clos depuis le mois de mars.
Dès qu'il eut tourné la clé, l'odeur du couloir lui revint, intacte, insupportable.
Sur la table de la cuisine, quelqu'un avait laissé une lettre à son nom.
Il la retourna longuement entre ses doigts sans l'ouvrir.
Jadis, il eût déchiré l'enveloppe sur-le-champ ; il avait appris la patience, ou la peur.
Le vent poussa un volet contre le mur et le bruit le fit sursauter.
Il songea qu'il pouvait encore repartir, reprendre le train de dix-sept heures et ne jamais savoir.
Puis il s'assit, approcha la lampe et ouvrit la lettre.
Ce qu'il y lut ne le surprit pas ; c'est cela, précisément, qui lui fit le plus de mal.
passages.english:
The train set him down at Villebranche a little before noon, under a low sky that promised rain.
Nothing had changed, and yet everything seemed smaller to him: the station, the square, the two plane trees.
He put his suitcase down on the bench, then thought better of it and picked it up again at once.
Nobody was waiting for him; he had told nobody he was coming.
The street climbed towards the church, as in the old days, between façades that the sun had faded.
A woman was sweeping her doorstep; she raised her head, watched him go past and did not recognise him.
He felt a relief that he did not dare admit to himself.
In front of the house he stopped: the shutters had been closed since March.
As soon as he had turned the key, the smell of the hallway came back to him, intact, unbearable.
On the kitchen table, someone had left a letter addressed to him.
He turned it over and over between his fingers without opening it.
Once, he would have torn the envelope open on the spot; he had learned patience, or fear.
The wind pushed a shutter against the wall and the noise made him start.
He reflected that he could still leave again, take the five o'clock train and never know.
Then he sat down, drew the lamp closer and opened the letter.
What he read there did not surprise him; and that, precisely, was what hurt him most.

questions.prompt: Which verb form in the passage is a passé antérieur?
The woman sweeping her doorstep recognises the traveller.
« Jadis, il eût déchiré l'enveloppe sur-le-champ » means:
options: Once, he would have torn the envelope open at once.
Once, he tore the envelope open at once.
Once, he had to tear the envelope open.
Once, he was tearing the envelope open.
questions.answer: Once, he would have torn the envelope open at once.

lessons.title: Figures de style
lessons.description: Name and use the figures that give French prose its edge: metaphor, irony, litotes and euphemism.

blocks.heading: Comparaison and métaphore
blocks.body: A comparaison links two terms with an explicit tool: comme, tel, semblable à, on dirait, pareil à. A métaphore removes the tool and states the identification directly, which makes it far more forceful. When the same image is carried through several sentences, French calls it a métaphore filée — an extended metaphor.

examples.french: Sa colère montait comme une marée.
examples.english: His anger was rising like a tide.
examples.note: comparaison: the tool comme is visible

examples.french: Sa colère était une marée qui montait.
examples.english: His anger was a rising tide.
examples.note: métaphore: the tool has disappeared

examples.french: La ville, ce vieil animal fatigué, s'étirait sous la pluie.
examples.english: The city, that tired old animal, stretched itself under the rain.
examples.note: apposition is a very common metaphor slot

examples.french: Il naviguait dans le dossier, sondait chaque page, redoutait les récifs.
examples.english: He was navigating the file, sounding each page, dreading the reefs.
examples.note: métaphore filée: one nautical image runs through the sentence

examples.french: Un silence de plomb tomba sur la salle.
examples.english: A leaden silence fell over the room.
examples.note: the metaphor is carried by the complement de plomb

blocks.tip: In French criticism you say « l'auteur file la métaphore de la navigation » — the verb filer is the technical term for sustaining an image.

blocks.heading: Saying less to mean more: litote and euphémisme
blocks.body: The litote denies the opposite in order to affirm something strongly: ce n'est pas mauvais can mean it is excellent. The euphémisme replaces a harsh word with a gentler one, usually out of tact rather than emphasis. Both are everywhere in French, from novels to press releases, and both can be missed by a literal reader.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas si mal joué.
examples.english: That is really rather well played.
examples.note: litote: the denial is praise

examples.french: Je ne vous cacherai pas ma déception.
examples.english: I will not hide my disappointment from you.
examples.note: litote used to soften a reproach

examples.french: Il nous a quittés au printemps dernier.
examples.english: He passed away last spring.
examples.note: euphémisme for mourir

examples.french: L'entreprise procède à un ajustement de ses effectifs.
examples.english: The company is adjusting its workforce.
examples.note: corporate euphemism for layoffs

examples.french: Votre travail manque un peu de rigueur.
examples.english: Your work is a little short on rigour.
examples.note: euphémisme: the criticism is far more severe than it sounds

examples.french: Elle n'est pas sans talent.
examples.english: She is far from untalented.
examples.note: the ne ... pas sans construction is a litote factory

blocks.tip: A litote intensifies, a euphémisme attenuates. Ask yourself: is the speaker being modest, or merely polite? That is the whole difference.

blocks.heading: Irony, antiphrase and the pointed word
blocks.body: French irony usually works by antiphrase: saying the opposite of what you mean while letting intonation, punctuation or context betray you. In writing, the signals are exaggeration, an incongruous register, a suspiciously enthusiastic adjective or a well-placed « bien sûr ». Sarcasm is heavier and openly aggressive; irony keeps a straight face.

examples.french: Quelle brillante idée de partir sans carte !
examples.english: What a brilliant idea to leave without a map!
examples.note: antiphrase: brillante means the opposite

examples.french: Il est d'une modestie remarquable, comme chacun sait.
examples.english: He is remarkably modest, as everyone knows.
examples.note: the added clause turns praise into mockery

examples.french: On appréciera la finesse de l'argument.
examples.english: One will appreciate the subtlety of the argument.
examples.note: the impersonal on is a favourite ironic mask

examples.french: Voilà une réforme qui ne dérangera personne, surtout pas ses auteurs.
examples.english: Here is a reform that will disturb nobody, least of all its authors.
examples.note: the sting arrives in the final clause

examples.french: Bien sûr, tout cela n'a rien à voir avec l'argent.
examples.english: Of course, none of this has anything to do with money.
examples.note: bien sûr flags the irony

blocks.tip: Irony is a risk in a foreign language: if the reader misses the signal, you simply sound wrong. In exams, use it in commentary (« l'auteur ironise sur... ») rather than in your own argument.

items.example: Relevez les figures de style de ce paragraphe.
items.exampleEnglish: Identify the figures of speech in this paragraph.

items.example: La métaphore du naufrage traverse tout le chapitre.
items.exampleEnglish: The metaphor of the shipwreck runs through the whole chapter.

items.example: L'auteur construit une métaphore filée sur trois pages.
items.exampleEnglish: The author builds an extended metaphor over three pages.

items.example: La comparaison se reconnaît à l'outil « comme ».
items.exampleEnglish: A simile can be spotted by the word "comme".

items.example: Cette image du jardin revient à chaque chapitre.
items.exampleEnglish: This image of the garden returns in every chapter.

items.example: « Ce n'est pas rien » est une litote très courante.
items.exampleEnglish: "That's not nothing" is a very common litotes.

items.example: « Un plan social » est l'euphémisme consacré.
items.exampleEnglish: "A social plan" is the established euphemism.

items.example: « Mourir de faim » est une hyperbole du quotidien.
items.exampleEnglish: "To be starving to death" is an everyday hyperbole.

items.example: L'ironie de ce passage échappe souvent aux lecteurs pressés.
items.exampleEnglish: The irony of this passage often escapes hurried readers.

items.example: « Bravo ! » est ici une antiphrase.
items.exampleEnglish: "Bravo!" is an antiphrasis here.

items.example: « Une douce violence » est un oxymore.
items.exampleEnglish: "A gentle violence" is an oxymoron.

items.example: La personnification du fleuve donne vie au paysage.
items.exampleEnglish: The personification of the river brings the landscape to life.

items.example: Le récit se lit comme une allégorie du pouvoir.
items.exampleEnglish: The story reads like an allegory of power.

items.english: metonymy (the part named for the whole)
items.example: « Boire un verre » est une métonymie banale.
items.exampleEnglish: "To drink a glass" is a commonplace metonymy.

items.example: « La Ville lumière » est une périphrase pour Paris.
items.exampleEnglish: "The City of Light" is a periphrasis for Paris.

items.english: anaphora, repetition at the start of clauses
items.example: L'anaphore de « jamais » martèle le discours.
items.exampleEnglish: The anaphora of "never" hammers the speech home.

items.example: La gradation conduit du murmure au cri.
items.exampleEnglish: The gradation leads from a whisper to a shout.

items.example: Le chiasme donne à la phrase un équilibre de miroir.
items.exampleEnglish: The chiasmus gives the sentence a mirror-like balance.

items.example: L'antithèse ombre / lumière structure le poème.
items.exampleEnglish: The shadow / light antithesis structures the poem.

items.example: L'allitération en s imite le sifflement du vent.
items.exampleEnglish: The alliteration in s imitates the hiss of the wind.

items.example: Une assonance en ou adoucit tout le vers.
items.exampleEnglish: An assonance in ou softens the whole line.

items.example: « Monter en haut » est un pléonasme.
items.exampleEnglish: "To go up upstairs" is a pleonasm.

items.example: Ce procédé stylistique crée une impression de vertige.
items.exampleEnglish: This stylistic device creates a feeling of dizziness.

items.example: Cette tournure appartient au registre soutenu.
items.exampleEnglish: This turn of phrase belongs to the formal register.

items.example: L'hyperbole exagère pour mieux frapper l'esprit.

items.example: L'euphémisme atténue la brutalité du propos.

items.english: to evoke, to call to mind
items.example: Cette image évoque la fuite du temps.

items.example: L'auteur ne démontre pas : il suggère.
items.exampleEnglish: The author does not demonstrate: he suggests.

items.example: La métaphore assimile la foule à un fleuve.
items.exampleEnglish: The metaphor likens the crowd to a river.

blocks.heading: The constructions figures are built on
blocks.body: Most figures rest on a small number of grammatical moulds. Similes need an outil de comparaison; litotes need a double negation; emphasis needs a dislocation or a cleft. Learning the mould lets you produce the figure rather than merely recognise it.

examples.french: Tel un vieil acteur, le maire salua la foule.
examples.english: Like an old actor, the mayor greeted the crowd.
examples.note: tel agrees with the noun that follows: tel un acteur, telle une reine

examples.french: On dirait une répétition générale.
examples.english: It looks like a dress rehearsal.
examples.note: on dirait + noun: the spoken simile

examples.french: Il n'est pas sans savoir que le dossier est vide.
examples.english: He is well aware that the file is empty.
examples.note: ne ... pas sans = a litotes of politeness

examples.french: Ce n'est pas tous les jours que l'on entend pareille franchise.
examples.english: It is not every day that one hears such frankness.
examples.note: cleft construction c'est ... que for emphasis

examples.french: Ce qui frappe, dans ce texte, c'est le silence des personnages.
examples.english: What strikes you in this text is the silence of the characters.
examples.note: ce qui ... c'est: the standard mise en relief

examples.french: Bavard, il l'était ; sincère, beaucoup moins.
examples.english: Talkative he certainly was; sincere, far less so.
examples.note: fronting the adjective creates an antithesis

blocks.tip: In a commentaire composé, always name the mould and then its effect: « la mise en relief souligne l'isolement du personnage ». Naming alone earns no marks.

blocks.heading: Repetition as an instrument
blocks.body: French rhetoric loves controlled repetition. The anaphore repeats the same word at the start of successive clauses; the gradation stacks terms of increasing intensity; the chiasme reverses the order of two paired elements to close a sentence on itself. All three are common in speeches, editorials and literary prose.

examples.french: Rien ne bougeait, rien ne parlait, rien ne semblait vivre.
examples.english: Nothing moved, nothing spoke, nothing seemed alive.
examples.note: anaphore of rien

examples.french: Il fut surpris, puis inquiet, puis franchement terrifié.
examples.english: He was surprised, then anxious, then frankly terrified.
examples.note: gradation ascendante

examples.french: Il faut manger pour vivre et non vivre pour manger.
examples.english: One must eat to live and not live to eat.
examples.note: chiasme: manger-vivre / vivre-manger

examples.french: Un homme sans passé, un passé sans témoin.
examples.english: A man without a past, a past without a witness.
examples.note: chiasme built on two nouns

examples.french: Ni la loi, ni l'usage, ni la morale n'y changeront rien.
examples.english: Neither the law, nor custom, nor morality will change anything about it.
examples.note: the triple ni gives the sentence a rhetorical rhythm

blocks.tip: French oratory favours the ternary rhythm — three parallel elements. Two feels unfinished, four feels like a list.

items.tip: Mark a short pause at each comma; the three verbs form a ternary rhythm that carries the image.

passages.title: Portrait d'un homme raisonnable
passages.french:
On disait de lui qu'il était un homme raisonnable, ce qui, dans notre ville, n'est pas un mince compliment.
Il n'avait jamais pris de risque, jamais élevé la voix, jamais déçu personne : quelle existence exemplaire !
Sa maison était un coffre-fort : rien n'y entrait, rien n'en sortait, pas même un mot plus haut que l'autre.
Chaque matin, il pliait ses convictions avec ses chemises et les rangeait dans le même tiroir.
Ses voisins l'admiraient ; ils n'auraient su dire pourquoi, et lui non plus.
Quand on lui demandait son avis, il répondait que la question méritait réflexion, et la réflexion durait des années.
« Ce n'est pas faux », disait-il des idées qu'il jugeait absurdes : c'était sa manière de ne fâcher personne.
Un jour, pourtant, la mer entra dans le coffre-fort.
Une lettre, une seule, suffit à faire céder les cloisons.
On ne sut jamais qui l'avait écrite, ni ce qu'elle contenait exactement.
Il devint distrait, puis silencieux, puis introuvable.
Ses collègues parlèrent d'un « repositionnement personnel » ; les journaux, d'une disparition.
Sa femme, elle, ne dit rien : elle avait toujours su que les coffres-forts finissent par rouiller.
Il reparut au printemps, amaigri, souriant, léger comme un homme qui a tout perdu, y compris la peur.
La ville lui trouva mauvaise mine et bonne conscience.
Depuis, on ne le dit plus raisonnable ; on dit seulement qu'il est enfin devenu lui-même.
passages.english:
People said of him that he was a reasonable man, which, in our town, is no small compliment.
He had never taken a risk, never raised his voice, never disappointed anyone: what an exemplary life!
His house was a safe: nothing came in, nothing went out, not even a raised word.
Every morning he folded his convictions along with his shirts and put them away in the same drawer.
His neighbours admired him; they could not have said why, and neither could he.
When his opinion was asked for, he replied that the question deserved thought, and the thinking lasted for years.
"That is not untrue," he would say of ideas he considered absurd: it was his way of never annoying anyone.
One day, however, the sea got into the safe.
One letter, a single one, was enough to make the walls give way.
Nobody ever knew who had written it, nor exactly what it contained.
He became absent-minded, then silent, then untraceable.
His colleagues spoke of a "personal repositioning"; the newspapers, of a disappearance.
His wife said nothing: she had always known that safes end up rusting.
He reappeared in spring, thinner, smiling, light as a man who has lost everything, including fear.
The town found him looking ill and feeling righteous.
Since then, people no longer call him reasonable; they merely say he has at last become himself.

lessons.title: Lire entre les lignes
lessons.description: Detect what a French text implies rather than states: presupposition, tone and the author's hidden stance.

blocks.heading: Présupposé and sous-entendu
blocks.body: French analysis distinguishes two kinds of implicit content. The présupposé is carried by the words themselves and survives negation: « Il a cessé de fumer » presupposes that he used to smoke, whether you deny the sentence or not. The sous-entendu depends on the situation and on what the speaker wants you to infer; it can always be disowned with « je n'ai jamais dit ça ».

examples.french: Il a cessé de se plaindre.
examples.english: He has stopped complaining.
examples.note: présupposé: he used to complain

examples.french: Même Paul a compris.
examples.english: Even Paul understood.
examples.note: présupposé: Paul is not considered quick-witted

examples.french: Vous êtes venu, vous aussi ?
examples.english: You came too?
examples.note: sous-entendu: I did not expect you here

examples.french: Ce rapport a au moins le mérite d'exister.
examples.english: This report at least has the merit of existing.
examples.note: sous-entendu: it has no other merit

examples.french: Je constate que la réunion commence sans elle.
examples.english: I note that the meeting is starting without her.
examples.note: constater presupposes the fact and implies a reproach

examples.french: C'est vous qui avez rédigé cette note ?
examples.english: You are the one who wrote this memo?
examples.note: the cleft turns a question into an accusation

blocks.tip: Test for a présupposé: negate the sentence. « Il n'a pas cessé de fumer » still presupposes that he smoked. If the implication survives, it is presupposed, not merely suggested.

blocks.heading: Modalisation: how the author colours the facts
blocks.body: Modalisation is the set of traces the writer leaves of their own judgement: adverbs (certes, hélas, curieusement), modal verbs (devoir, pouvoir), the conditionnel of unverified information, quotation marks of distance, and above all the choice of reporting verbs. Two texts can carry identical facts and opposite stances.

examples.french: Le ministre affirme que la réforme est prête.
examples.english: The minister states that the reform is ready.
examples.note: affirmer: neutral report

examples.french: Le ministre prétend que la réforme est prête.
examples.english: The minister claims that the reform is ready.
examples.note: prétendre: the journalist doubts it

examples.french: Le ministre reconnaît que la réforme est prête.
examples.english: The minister concedes that the reform is ready.
examples.note: reconnaître implies it was reluctantly admitted

examples.french: Le suspect aurait quitté le pays dans la nuit.
examples.english: The suspect reportedly left the country during the night.
examples.note: conditionnel journalistique: unverified

examples.french: Cette prétendue « concertation » n'a duré qu'une heure.
examples.english: This so-called "consultation" lasted only an hour.
examples.note: prétendue + quotation marks = double distance

examples.french: Curieusement, le rapport ne cite aucun chiffre.
examples.english: Curiously, the report quotes no figures.
examples.note: one adverb turns an observation into a suspicion

blocks.tip: When you summarise a French text, keep its modalisation: writing « la réforme est prête » where the author wrote « prétend » already misrepresents the source.

blocks.heading: Where does the narrator stand?
blocks.body: In fiction, focalisation tells you whose eyes you are looking through: zéro (an omniscient narrator who knows everything), interne (we are limited to one character's perceptions), externe (we see only behaviour, as through a camera). The discours indirect libre blends the narrator's voice with the character's thoughts without any introducing verb — the surest way to make a reader share a judgement without stating it.

examples.french: Elle ignorait que l'homme la suivait depuis la gare.
examples.english: She did not know that the man had been following her since the station.
examples.note: focalisation zéro: the narrator knows more than the character

examples.french: Il lui sembla que la pièce avait rétréci.
examples.english: It seemed to him that the room had shrunk.
examples.note: focalisation interne: filtered through one consciousness

examples.french: L'homme posa son verre, se leva et sortit sans un mot.
examples.english: The man put down his glass, got up and went out without a word.
examples.note: focalisation externe: behaviour only, no thoughts

examples.french: Elle relut la lettre. Non, décidément, cet homme ne changerait jamais.
examples.english: She reread the letter. No, this man really would never change.
examples.note: discours indirect libre: her voice inside the narration

examples.french: Il accepta l'invitation. Après tout, que risquait-il ?
examples.english: He accepted the invitation. After all, what was he risking?
examples.note: the question belongs to the character, not the narrator

blocks.tip: In a commentaire, do not confuse l'auteur with le narrateur. The narrator is a construction; the ironic distance between the two is often the whole point of the text.

items.english: the implicit, what is not said outright
items.example: Tout le sens du texte se joue dans l'implicite.
items.exampleEnglish: The whole meaning of the text is played out in what is implied.

items.example: L'auteur reste allusif : rien n'est explicite.
items.exampleEnglish: The author remains allusive: nothing is explicit.

items.example: Sa réponse est pleine de sous-entendus.
items.exampleEnglish: His answer is full of innuendo.

items.example: La question repose sur un présupposé contestable.
items.exampleEnglish: The question rests on a debatable presupposition.

items.example: Le non-dit pèse plus lourd que les paroles.
items.exampleEnglish: What goes unsaid weighs more than the words.

items.example: L'allusion à la guerre n'est jamais formulée clairement.
items.exampleEnglish: The allusion to the war is never clearly spelled out.

items.example: Le mot « régime » a ici une connotation péjorative.
items.exampleEnglish: The word "regime" here has a pejorative connotation.

items.example: La dénotation est neutre ; la connotation, jamais.
items.exampleEnglish: Denotation is neutral; connotation never is.

items.example: Le ton du passage devient franchement polémique.
items.exampleEnglish: The tone of the passage becomes frankly polemical.

items.example: La modalisation trahit le scepticisme du journaliste.
items.exampleEnglish: The modalisation betrays the journalist's scepticism.

items.example: « Hélas » est un modalisateur d'opinion.
items.exampleEnglish: "Alas" is a modalising word expressing opinion.

items.example: La focalisation interne nous enferme dans sa conscience.
items.exampleEnglish: Internal focalisation locks us inside his consciousness.

items.example: Le point de vue change au milieu du chapitre.
items.exampleEnglish: The point of view shifts in the middle of the chapter.

items.example: Le discours indirect libre mêle la voix du narrateur et celle du personnage.
items.exampleEnglish: Free indirect speech blends the narrator's voice with the character's.

items.english: enunciation, the act of speaking in a text
items.example: Les marques d'énonciation révèlent un locuteur engagé.
items.exampleEnglish: The marks of enunciation reveal a committed speaker.

items.example: Le destinataire de ce pamphlet n'est pas le grand public.
items.exampleEnglish: The intended reader of this pamphlet is not the general public.

items.example: L'auteur laisse au lecteur le soin de conclure.
items.exampleEnglish: The author leaves the reader to draw the conclusion.

items.english: the aim, the purpose (of a text)
items.example: La visée du texte est manifestement polémique.
items.exampleEnglish: The aim of the text is plainly polemical.

items.example: L'article assume un parti pris qu'il ne cache pas.
items.exampleEnglish: The article takes a stance that it does not hide.

items.example: Sa prise de position a surpris jusqu'à ses proches.
items.exampleEnglish: His taking a stand surprised even those close to him.

items.example: Il approuve sans arrière-pensée.
items.exampleEnglish: He approves without any ulterior motive.

items.example: Les guillemets marquent une distance critique.
items.exampleEnglish: The quotation marks signal a critical distance.

items.example: Cette soi-disant neutralité ne trompe personne.
items.exampleEnglish: This so-called neutrality fools nobody.

items.example: Un document prétendument confidentiel circule déjà.
items.exampleEnglish: An allegedly confidential document is already circulating.

items.example: L'auteur vise vraisemblablement un lectorat averti.
items.exampleEnglish: The author is in all likelihood aiming at an informed readership.

items.example: Que sous-entendez-vous exactement ?
items.exampleEnglish: What exactly are you implying?

items.english: to give to understand, to insinuate
items.example: Le communiqué laisse entendre que la décision est prise.
items.exampleEnglish: The statement gives to understand that the decision has been made.

items.english: to detect, to pick up on
items.example: On décèle une pointe d'amertume dans ce paragraphe.
items.exampleEnglish: One detects a hint of bitterness in this paragraph.

items.example: Il est difficile de discerner la thèse de l'auteur.
items.exampleEnglish: It is hard to discern the author's thesis.

items.example: Il insinue sans jamais accuser franchement.
items.exampleEnglish: He insinuates without ever accusing openly.

items.example: L'article prétend rapporter les faits sans les commenter.
items.exampleEnglish: The article claims to report the facts without commenting on them.

items.example: L'éditorial martèle la même idée à chaque paragraphe.
items.exampleEnglish: The editorial hammers the same idea home in every paragraph.

items.english: to betray, to give away (a feeling)
items.example: Un seul adverbe trahit son agacement.
items.exampleEnglish: A single adverb gives away his irritation.

items.example: La fin du roman reste volontairement ambiguë.
items.exampleEnglish: The end of the novel remains deliberately ambiguous.

items.example: Sa réponse équivoque n'engage à rien.
items.exampleEnglish: His equivocal answer commits him to nothing.

items.example: Le narrateur adopte un ton désabusé.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrator adopts a disillusioned tone.

blocks.heading: Le discours indirect libre
blocks.body: Free indirect speech keeps the tenses and pronouns of indirect speech (imparfait, conditionnel, third person) but drops the introducing verb and the subordinating que. The result is a sentence that is grammatically the narrator's and psychologically the character's. Watch for exclamations, questions and colloquial words inside an otherwise literary narration.

examples.french: Direct : « Je ne reviendrai jamais ici », pensa-t-il.
examples.english: Direct: "I shall never come back here," he thought.

examples.french: Indirect : Il pensa qu'il ne reviendrait jamais là.
examples.english: Indirect: He thought that he would never come back there.

examples.french: Indirect libre : Il regarda la maison une dernière fois. Il ne reviendrait jamais.
examples.english: Free indirect: He looked at the house one last time. He would never come back.
examples.note: no verb of thought, no que — but the voice is his

examples.french: Elle ouvrit l'enveloppe. Encore une facture ! Décidément, ce mois-ci ne finirait jamais.
examples.english: She opened the envelope. Another bill! This month really was never going to end.
examples.note: the exclamation and décidément belong to the character

examples.french: Il hésita. Fallait-il vraiment lui dire la vérité ?
examples.english: He hesitated. Did he really have to tell her the truth?
examples.note: a question with no quotation marks: the character's own

blocks.tip: Two clues betray free indirect speech: a conditional where you expected a future, and an exclamation or question with no quotation marks and no verb of speech.

blocks.heading: Marking distance from what you report
blocks.body: French offers a graded scale for reporting something you do not endorse: the conditionnel of unverified news, the adjectives prétendu and soi-disant, the adverb prétendument, quotation marks of distance and the verb prétendre. Each degree tells the reader how far the writer stands back.

examples.french: Selon plusieurs sources, l'accord serait déjà signé.
examples.english: According to several sources, the agreement is said to be already signed.
examples.note: conditionnel: information not confirmed

examples.french: Le prétendu expert n'a publié aucun travail sur le sujet.
examples.english: The so-called expert has published no work on the subject.
examples.note: prétendu precedes the noun and denies the title

examples.french: On nous promet une « révolution » du secteur.
examples.english: We are promised a "revolution" in the sector.
examples.note: quotation marks alone convey the irony

examples.french: Il aurait, dit-on, refusé le poste.
examples.english: He reportedly turned down the position.
examples.note: dit-on adds a second layer of caution

examples.french: Loin de moi l'idée de contester ces chiffres.
examples.english: Far be it from me to dispute these figures.
examples.note: a formula that announces the contestation that follows

blocks.tip: Never translate the conditionnel journalistique with a plain past in English: « le suspect aurait fui » is "the suspect allegedly fled", not "the suspect fled". The difference is legal as well as stylistic.

items.tip: Give serait a slight lift in pitch — that is where a French listener hears the caution.

items.prompt: Say this sentence so that the reproach is audible but unspoken.

items.prompt: Introduce a criticism politely before making it.

items.english: Far be it from me to dispute these figures, but their source remains obscure.
items.tip: Pause after chiffres; the whole rhetorical effect depends on that hinge before mais.

passages.title: Un roman qui ne manque pas d'ambition
passages.french:
Le nouveau roman de Clara Vasseur paraît cette semaine, précédé d'une rumeur flatteuse que son éditeur n'a pas jugé utile de démentir.
Le livre, nous dit-on, aurait été écrit en trois mois ; on veut bien le croire.
L'ambition, en tout cas, ne lui fait pas défaut : six cents pages, quatre générations, deux continents.
On y trouve de belles pages, notamment celles où l'autrice consent à décrire plutôt qu'à expliquer.
Le chapitre de l'incendie n'est d'ailleurs pas indigne des meilleurs récits du genre.
Le reste appelle quelques réserves, que la critique, unanime, s'est jusqu'ici abstenue de formuler.
Les personnages secondaires, prétendument « inoubliables », ont la fâcheuse habitude de disparaître dès qu'ils cessent d'être utiles.
Quant au narrateur, il sait tout, explique tout et, par précaution, le répète.
On aimerait qu'il fît parfois confiance à son lecteur.
Ce n'est pas que le style manque de qualités : il en a, et il tient à ce qu'on le sache.
Chaque métaphore semble réclamer son salaire ; aucune ne travaille en silence.
L'ouvrage a déjà été salué comme « le grand roman de notre décennie », formule dont on remarquera qu'elle n'engage que ceux qui la reçoivent.
Il se vendra, vraisemblablement, fort bien.
Faut-il pour autant le déconseiller ? Certainement pas.
On le lira avec plaisir, en sautant quelques pages, comme on lit les romans qui ont eu la chance de plaire avant d'être lus.
Et l'on attendra le suivant, sans impatience excessive.
passages.english:
Clara Vasseur's new novel comes out this week, preceded by a flattering rumour that her publisher has not seen fit to deny.
The book, we are told, was reportedly written in three months; we are quite willing to believe it.
Ambition, at any rate, is not lacking: six hundred pages, four generations, two continents.
There are fine pages in it, notably those where the author consents to describe rather than to explain.
The chapter of the fire is, incidentally, not unworthy of the best narratives of the genre.
The rest calls for a few reservations, which the critics, unanimous, have so far refrained from voicing.
The secondary characters, allegedly "unforgettable", have the unfortunate habit of vanishing as soon as they stop being useful.
As for the narrator, he knows everything, explains everything and, as a precaution, repeats it.
One would like him to trust his reader now and then.
It is not that the style lacks qualities: it has them, and it insists that you know it.
Every metaphor seems to be demanding its wages; not one of them works in silence.
The book has already been hailed as "the great novel of our decade", a formula which, one may note, commits only those who accept it.
It will, in all likelihood, sell very well.
Should one therefore advise against it? Certainly not.
It will be read with pleasure, skipping a few pages, the way one reads novels that have had the luck to please before being read.
And we shall await the next one, without excessive impatience.
